echoes.note: The Pharisees and scribes 'murmured' (diegongyzon) that Jesus eats with sinners; LXX uses gongyzo precisely for Israel's murmuring against God's provision in the wilderness. Luke evokes the recurrent grumbling motif to cast the objectors as faithless Israel resisting God's gracious feeding. Coherence is strong because the parables that follow defend a divine table.

The separatist who says 'Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am holier than you' supplies the exact posture Luke's Pharisees adopt against table fellowship with sinners. Isaiah condemns this self-segregating holiness as a stench before God, which coheres with Jesus' vindication of welcoming sinners. Availability and thematic coherence are high; verbal overlap is thematic rather than lexical.

The wisdom ideal that the righteous do not sit with sinners frames the Pharisees' assumption that eating with sinners defiles. Luke inverts the maxim: Jesus' table redefines blessedness as seeking rather than separating. Faint and contested, resting on shared sinner/righteous vocabulary.

God declares 'I myself will search for my sheep... I will seek the lost,' the precise plot of the one shepherd who leaves the flock to find the strayed (vv. 4,6,16). Volume is high (sustained seeking-shepherd oracle), recurrence strong (Ezekiel 34 is a touchstone for Luke's shepherd Christology), and coherence exact: God's own searching contrasts the failed shepherds, just as Jesus seeks sinners the Pharisees abandon.

The shepherd who gathers lambs and carries them in his bosom illuminates the man carrying the found sheep on his shoulders rejoicing. The tender carrying gesture is distinctive and shared, strengthening the divine-shepherd reading. Coheres with Ezekiel 34 as the comfort-of-God shepherd image.

'I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant' supplies the penitent's voice answered by the seeking shepherd. The verbal pairing of straying sheep and divine seeking is close, and coherence with the repentance emphasis (v.7) is strong. Slightly lower volume than Ezekiel 34.

'All we like sheep have gone astray, we have turned every one to his own way' is the canonical image of straying that the parable assumes for 'one sinner who repents.' Recurrence in Luke's passion theology supports availability; the echo is thematic rather than cited here. Contested as to whether Luke intends the Servant song specifically.

The woe on shepherds who scatter and the promise that God will gather the remnant and set true shepherds over them stands behind the lost-sheep rescue. Coheres with Ezekiel 34 as the prophetic indictment of leaders who fail the flock, paralleling the Pharisees. Lower volume, so an echo.

God's promise to gather the remnant of Israel 'like sheep in a fold' supplies the regathering motif. Faint and one of several gathering oracles; included for recurrence within the shepherd-restoration cluster. Contested because no distinctive verbal link to a single lost sheep.

The flock doomed to slaughter and the shepherd's care/abandonment drama belongs to the same prophetic shepherd field Luke draws on. Faint here; included as availability for the seeking-shepherd theme. Contested.

God 'searches Jerusalem with lamps' to find the complacent, a near image to the woman lighting a lamp and sweeping to find the coin. The lamp-search vocabulary is suggestive, though Zephaniah's search is judicial, here gracious. Contested and faint.

Seeking wisdom 'as silver, and searching for it as for hidden treasure' parallels the diligent search for the lost silver drachma until found. The seek-until-found wisdom pattern coheres with the parable's diligence, but the link is thematic. Contested.

The beloved who seeks through the night 'until I found him' and then summons others to rejoice mirrors the woman's seek-find-celebrate structure. Faint, figural, contested; included as a seek-and-find availability rather than a deliberate citation.

The law of inheritance giving the firstborn a double portion frames 'give me my share of your property' and the father's division between the two sons. The legal background makes the younger son's premature demand pointed and the father's later 'all that is mine is yours' (v.31) the firstborn's lawful due. Coherence high; verbal link thematic.

The patriarchal pattern of departing to a far country when 'a severe famine' strikes the land underlies the son's far-country famine. The famine-driven sojourn is a recurrent Genesis motif (also 26:1; 41-47), lending availability. Contested as a specific source; an ambient echo.

The pig is declared unclean, so feeding swine and craving their husks marks the Jewish son's total degradation and ritual estrangement. For a Torah-formed audience the swine signal maximal defilement, intensifying the depth from which the father's mercy reaches. Volume modest but coherence and distinctiveness high.

'Whoever loves wisdom makes his father glad, but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth' compactly anticipates both the prodigal's wasteful living and the elder son's accusation of harlots (v.30). The proverb pairs squandering and harlotry with a father, exactly Luke's configuration. Coherence strong.

'Do not give yourself to prostitutes, lest you lose your inheritance' (deuterocanonical wisdom) joins squandering to harlotry and lost inheritance, the prodigal's exact fall. Availability within Second-Temple wisdom strengthens the moral frame. Contested and faint as a direct source.

Pharaoh's 'I have sinned against the LORD your God, and against you' is the closest verbal template for 'I have sinned against heaven, and in your sight,' the dual against-God-and-against-you formula. The parallel sharpens the son's confession as a recognized penitential script. Contested between this and the Davidic confessions.

'Against you, you only, have I sinned, and done what is evil in your sight' supplies the language of sinning before God's sight that the son rehearses. As the paradigmatic penitential psalm it carries high recurrence in Jewish repentance piety, cohering with Luke's repentance theme (vv.7,10). Distinctive 'in your sight' overlap.

David's terse 'I have sinned against the LORD' models confession answered immediately by restoration, the rhythm of the son's resolve answered by the father. Recurrence of the 'I have sinned' formula across Saul/David/Pharaoh makes any single attribution contested. Faint.

Esau 'ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, and kissed him, and they wept' is the precise gesture-cluster of the father who ran, fell on his neck, and kissed the returning son. Volume and verbal distinctiveness are very high (run + fall on neck + kiss in sequence), and coherence is strong: an estranged brother/son reunion of unexpected mercy.

Joseph falling on his brothers' necks, weeping and kissing them, reinforces the reconciliation embrace, and the broader Joseph reunion (46:29, falling on Jacob's neck) supplies the lost-then-found-alive frame. Recurrence of the Joseph story across this pericope (robe, ring, 'dead/alive') is strong. Slightly lower verbal match than Genesis 33:4.

Pharaoh exalts Joseph by putting a ring on his hand and clothing him in fine robes, the exact pair of honors (best robe + ring) the father bestows. The Joseph parallel makes the restored son a reinstated heir, not merely a forgiven servant. Distinctive robe-and-ring combination yields high volume and coherence.

Joshua the high priest has his filthy garments removed and is clothed in rich robes as a sign of restored standing, illuminating the 'best robe' that re-clothes the defiled son. The figural logic of imputed honor replacing defilement coheres tightly with the swine-defiled returnee. Verbal link is the robe of restoration.

Abraham's slaughter of a choice, tender calf for honored guests supplies the cultural background of the fattened calf killed for celebration. Faint and one of several calf-feast scenes (1 Samuel 28:24); included for the hospitality-feast availability. Contested.

Jacob mourns Joseph as dead and refuses comfort, so that Joseph's later disclosure that he is alive (45:26-28) is the canonical 'was dead and is alive, was lost and is found' reversal the father proclaims. The figural fit of a father's lost-and-restored son is strong and recurs across this pericope's Joseph allusions. Lower verbal volume, hence figural.

Jonah is angry at God's mercy to the undeserving, sulks outside, and God comes out reasoning with him to the parable's open end, exactly the elder son angry at mercy whom the father comes out and entreats, ending on an unanswered appeal. Coherence is very high (resentment at grace, divine entreaty, open conclusion) and the structural parallel is distinctive. A strong figural-allusive frame for Luke's audience of grumblers.

Cain is angry and downcast over a brother's favored standing, and the LORD comes out to him with entreaty and warning, paralleling the elder brother's anger and the father's coming out to plead. The elder-resents-younger pattern is the primal sibling-rivalry script. Coherence good; verbal link thematic.

The law of the stubborn and rebellious son who is gluttonous and a drunkard, to be brought before the elders and stoned, is the dark legal backdrop the parable deliberately subverts: the father runs to embrace rather than condemn. Directly preceding the inheritance law (21:17) already echoed, strengthening recurrence. Coherence high as a subverted intertext.

Esau's bitter outcry and resentment over a blessing/inheritance given to the younger brother colors the elder son's grievance about service and unrewarded faithfulness. Recurrence of the older-brother-aggrieved motif (Cain, Esau) supports availability; verbal link is faint. Contested.

The elder son's charge that the younger 'devoured your living with prostitutes' restates Proverbs' 'companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth,' tying the two parts of the parable together with one wisdom maxim. Recurrence with 15:13 makes the proverb a coherent through-line. Verbal overlap of squandering plus harlotry.
